survivors.rationale:
_stale_pid_check is the acquire()-side STALE-LOCK-FILE HYGIENE helper. Before
opening the lock, connect_write calls it to read the sidecar's stamped PID and,
if that process is DEAD (``os.kill(pid, 0)`` raises ProcessLookupError /
PermissionError), unlink the ORPHANED LOCK FILE the dead holder left behind —
the file plus its stamped PID/purpose/timestamp (runtime/db_lock.py:68-94). Its
own docstring is explicit: "The OS releases the flock on process death, but the
lock file and its PID stamp persist. This is a best-effort hygiene helper ... the
real serialization still happens via flock." No-op-ing the ``os.kill(pid, 0)``
probe makes the dead-holder branch never fire, so the orphaned lock file + its
stale stamp are NEVER cleaned up. The OBSERVABLE EFFECT is exactly that: a stale
``<db>.write.lock`` (still naming the crashed PID/purpose) lingers on disk and
``cat``-ing it for diagnosis points at a dead process. It is NOT a deadlock — the
OS auto-released the flock on death and connect_write re-creates the file via
``os.open(lock_path, O_CREAT | O_WRONLY)`` at line 280, so a NEW writer acquires
the flock on the persisted file whether or not the stale one was unlinked. The
selector points at tests/test_retrieval_time_gate.py, a clean, collectable suite
that exercises connect_write (so it imports + uses db_lock for real, not via
mocks) — but NO test in the tree drives a DEAD-PID stale-file cleanup (grep for
_stale_pid_check / orphan-lock found none). EXPECTED: this SURVIVES — the finding
is an under-tested HYGIENE path, NOT a tool bug. The worklist item is a real
stale-lock-FILE-cleanup behavior test: stamp the sidecar lock file with a DEAD
pid, call connect_write, and assert the orphaned lock file is RECLAIMED/cleaned
(unlinked then re-created with this writer's stamp) — NOT "assert the pipeline
doesn't deadlock" (it never would). Do NOT write it here (out of scope — it is a
product-test owner's call).
